A.title: ACMA Payment Blocking Guidance: Banks' Section 15J Duty
A.excerpt: From 1 January 2027, Australian banks and payment firms must block transfers to illegal gambling. ACMA's guidance says blocklists are not enough.
body: The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) published its initial guidance on 17 November 2026 for the new payment-blocking duty in section 15J of the Interactive Gambling Act 2001. The provision, inserted by the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Act 2026, takes effect on 1 January 2027. From that date, authorised deposit-taking institutions and payment-system participants must take reasonably practicable steps to prevent transfers to designated interactive gambling services. The guidance's central message is blunt: firms that wait for the regulator to flag individual operators will not meet the standard.

The scope of the duty is wide. Designated services are prohibited interactive gambling services, such as online casinos and online slots, which cannot lawfully be offered to Australians, and unlicensed regulated services, such as wagering or lotteries offered without a state or territory licence. The duty applies whether the service is based in Australia or offshore, and 'funds' expressly includes digital units of value, including cryptocurrency. ACMA lists banks, credit unions, digital wallet and payment service providers, card schemes, gateways, acquirers, processors and crypto service providers as entities that may be caught, depending on their role in the payment chain. Payouts of winnings to Australian customers are not covered.

For enforcement purposes, the most significant passage is ACMA's statement that 'reliance on ACMA information alone is unlikely to be sufficient to identify all relevant transactions.' The regulator's blocked-site list and the licensing registers are described as starting points, not a safe harbour. This moves the obligation from a reactive, list-matching exercise to a risk-based framework closer to anti-money laundering compliance. Firms will be expected to document an initial risk assessment covering how likely relevant transfers are and how much visibility and control they have, approve it through proper governance, and translate it into controls that are tested and reviewed.

ACMA also closes off the outsourcing argument. Relying on another participant in the payment chain, or on a third-party compliance vendor, does not on its own discharge the section 15J obligation. An acquirer cannot assume the card scheme will catch the problem, and a wallet provider cannot assume the issuing bank will. Each entity will be judged on its own role, the information available to it, the cost and capability of the controls open to it, and the quality of its decision records. That flexible standard is helpful to smaller firms, but it also means there is no single compliance template that will satisfy the regulator.

The suggested controls will be familiar to payments compliance teams: merchant category code screening, analysis of merchant and account data, blacklists of known illegal services and whitelists of licensed operators, rules-based transaction monitoring, information-sharing arrangements, staff training, audits and independent reviews. ACMA has also published draft payment-flow diagrams for card, alternative payment (including buy now pay later, prepaid vouchers and digital wallets) and cryptocurrency pathways, with blockchain data attribution screening identified for the latter. Because offshore operators routinely change payment routes, descriptors and identifiers, ACMA stresses that controls must be updated regularly rather than set once.

There are open questions. The guidance does not set out how ACMA will approach breaches in practice, and it signals that formal guidance under section 15K may follow. The interaction with miscoding by offshore merchants, payment facilitators that aggregate many sub-merchants, and crypto on-ramps that do not see the end destination of funds will test the 'reasonably practicable' standard. Firms should expect that ACMA's earliest enforcement attention will focus on whether a credible, documented risk assessment existed at commencement, rather than on whether every single transaction was stopped.

The reform also matters for licensed operators. Wagering providers holding Australian state or territory licences should ensure they are correctly identified on whitelists and merchant data so that legitimate deposits are not caught by over-blocking. Offshore operators holding licences elsewhere should note ACMA's position that a foreign licence does not authorise service to Australians. With just six weeks until commencement, payment firms with Australian exposure should finalise risk assessments, confirm board-level approval, map their payment flows against ACMA's diagrams and respond to the consultation on the draft materials. Specialist gambling and payments counsel can assist with gap analyses ahead of 1 January 2027.

A.title: Ashton v TSE Malta: Betfair Duty of Care Claim Fails
A.excerpt: The High Court rejects a broad duty on operators to intervene in problem gambling but leaves a narrow route to liability open. What it means.
body: On 13 November 2026, Mr Justice Swift handed down judgment in Ashton and others v TSE Malta LP [2026] EWHC 2935 (KB), dismissing a negligence claim brought against the operator of the Betfair Exchange by the family of Luke Ashton, who died in April 2021. The claim, brought under the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1934 and the Fatal Accidents Act 1976, alleged that the operator failed to prevent or respond to gambling-related harm that worsened Mr Ashton's gambling disorder. It was the most closely watched gambling tort case in England for nearly two decades, and the outcome will shape litigation risk for every operator licensed by the Gambling Commission.

The headline holding is that there is no broad common-law duty on gambling operators to intervene whenever a customer shows markers of problem gambling, including any general duty to 'offer assistance.' The judge gave significant weight to personal autonomy and to the incremental way in which new duties of care develop. He distinguished the operator-customer relationship from relationships, such as employment, in which protective duties are more readily found. The claimants' core strategy of importing the Commission's social responsibility standards wholesale into the content of a tortious duty was rejected.

Central to that conclusion was section 24(8) of the Gambling Act 2005, which provides that a breach of a Commission code of practice does not of itself make a person liable to civil proceedings. The court treated this as a clear signal that Parliament intended regulatory standards to be enforced by the regulator, not through private damages claims. The judge also observed that the regulatory framework addresses a much wider category of gambling-related harm than the recognised psychiatric injury that negligence law protects against. Regulatory non-compliance may still have some evidential relevance, but it does not create a cause of action.

The judgment does not give operators complete comfort. Building on Calvert v William Hill Credit Ltd [2008] EWHC 454 (Ch), the court accepted that a narrower duty may arise in exceptional circumstances: a duty to act to prevent gambling disorder in its severe form where that is foreseeable. Three routes were identified: where the operator has notice of a diagnosed gambling disorder; where the customer's behaviour is so extreme that it demonstrates a total lack of control; and where the operator has voluntarily assumed responsibility, for example by agreeing to implement a self-exclusion request and then failing to do so. Those categories map closely onto information operators already hold through their safer gambling and affordability processes.

The case ultimately turned on the evidence. The claimants' expert considered that Mr Ashton met eight of the nine DSM-5 criteria for severe gambling disorder; the defendant's expert found two criteria met, one possibly met and insufficient evidence for the rest. The judge preferred the defence evidence and held that betting records alone cannot reliably establish a clinical diagnosis, which requires a history and information about the person's feelings and motivations. Because severe gambling disorder was not established, and the operator could not be shown to have known or ought to have known of that risk, the duty did not arise on the facts.

For compliance teams, the practical lessons are twofold. First, the judgment confirms that the primary consequence of social responsibility failings remains regulatory: Commission enforcement, settlements and licence reviews are unaffected, and the decision expressly does not displace duties under the 2005 Act. Second, the narrow duty means that what an operator actually knows matters. Records of customer disclosures, self-exclusion requests, interactions triggered by extreme play and third-party notifications of a diagnosis are precisely the facts that could bring an operator within the exceptional categories. Operators should ensure that such information is escalated and acted on promptly, and that self-exclusion and account-closure commitments are honoured without exception.

Claimant firms will study the judgment for an appeal route, and similar claims are pending against other operators, so the law may yet move. For now, the decision gives UK licensees, including Malta-based groups serving the British market, a clearer picture: civil liability is the exception, not the rule, but it is triggered by knowledge and assumed responsibility. Operators should review their safer gambling escalation procedures and record-keeping in light of the three routes the court identified, ideally with input from specialist gambling litigation and regulatory counsel.

A.title: Alberta Clears AGLC to Sell Play Alberta: What It Means
A.excerpt: An Order in Council lets AGLC sell Play Alberta and its player accounts. We examine the privacy guardrails and what buyers must accept.
body: Alberta has taken a formal step towards separating its gambling regulator from its online gambling operation. On 13 November 2026, Lieutenant Governor Salma Lakhani signed an Order in Council permitting Alberta Gaming, Liquor and Cannabis (AGLC) to sell Play Alberta, including its data and player accounts, to an outside company. Dale Nally, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction, issued a statement on 16 November confirming the authority but stressing that no sale decision has been made. AGLC is reported to be in discussions with potential purchasers.

The move follows the launch of Alberta's open, competitive iGaming market on 13 July 2026. Before that date, Play Alberta was the province's only legal online casino and sports betting option. By mid-November, 30 licensed operators were running 51 websites in the province. That growth has exposed the structural tension the minister identified: whether AGLC should continue both to regulate the market and to compete in it through its own platform, or whether it should focus solely on compliance, responsible gambling and player protection. A sale would leave AGLC's regulatory role intact.

For prospective buyers, the asset is attractive principally because of its customer base. AGLC reported more than 434,000 registered Play Alberta accounts as of October 2025, an established player pool that new entrants in a freshly opened market would otherwise need to acquire through costly marketing. However, the Order in Council attaches conditions that shape both valuation and deal structure. Any new owner must enter into an operating agreement with the Alberta iGaming Corporation (AiGC), the body that contracts with private operators in the new market, and must handle personal information in accordance with Alberta's Protection of Privacy Act, as AGLC does today.

The player-account transfer rules are the most legally significant guardrail. Players must receive advance notice of changes, and those who wish to opt out will have at least 90 days to decline the transfer of their accounts. Accounts of players who opt out, and of players enrolled in self-exclusion, will not be transferred. A buyer therefore cannot assume it will acquire the full registered base, and it will need to plan for a migration process with clear communications, verification of consent and robust data-handling controls. Deal documents will need to address what happens to the accounts and balances of players who do not transfer.

The self-exclusion carve-out raises a practical compliance point. Because self-excluded players will not move across, the buyer will need a reliable mechanism to ensure those individuals are not re-acquired through marketing or new registrations on the acquired platform. Operators entering Alberta should expect the AiGC and AGLC to scrutinise how any transferred data is reconciled against provincial self-exclusion records. Privacy counsel will also want to review the lawful basis for transferring account data from a public body to a private company and the scope of permitted downstream uses.

The development has wider significance for Canadian market entry. Ontario's model separated regulation from private operation from the outset, while other provinces continue to run government-operated monopolies. If Alberta proceeds, it would become the first province to privatise an existing government iGaming platform after liberalising its market, a precedent that could inform debates elsewhere as provinces such as Nova Scotia and New Brunswick consider their own online gambling frameworks. It also signals to licensed operators that the competitive field in Alberta may soon include a well-capitalised private owner of what was the incumbent brand.

Operators and investors considering a bid should begin diligence on the AiGC operating agreement terms, the privacy and consent mechanics of the account transfer, and any brand and technology licensing arrangements that may sit outside the sale. Existing Alberta licensees should monitor the process for its competitive implications. Canadian and cross-border gaming counsel experienced in the Ontario and Alberta frameworks can advise on transaction structure and regulatory approvals.

A.title: Senators Press CFTC to Reverse Prediction Market Geofencing
A.excerpt: Nine Senate Democrats demand the CFTC withdraw its 5 November geofencing interpretation and preserve records by 23 November.
body: The federal-state conflict over sports event contracts has moved to Capitol Hill. On 16 November 2026, Senator Adam Schiff and eight Democratic colleagues wrote to Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman Michael Selig urging the agency to withdraw its 5 November interpretation directing designated contract markets (DCMs) to stop geofencing certain event-contract markets. The co-signatories are Senators Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen of Nevada, Maria Cantwell and Patty Murray of Washington, Elissa Slotkin and Gary Peters of Michigan, Alex Padilla of California, and Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, the Ranking Member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the CFTC.

The senators' central complaint is that the interpretation effectively requires prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states and on all tribal lands, notwithstanding court orders in California, Michigan, Nevada and Washington requiring platforms to geofence their states or reservations. 'Your unilateral decision directly conflicts with active court orders, undermines state and tribal law, and must be reversed,' the letter states. It asks the Commission to withdraw the interpretation or freeze all implementation efforts until the litigation is resolved.

The letter also contains an oversight dimension that should not be overlooked. The CFTC has been asked to preserve all records and communications on the letter's subject matter from 1 January 2025 onward, and to confirm by 23 November that it is doing so. The senators suggest the agency may be coordinating with platforms that are themselves litigants. While a letter from minority senators carries no binding force, a records-preservation demand from the ranking member of the CFTC's oversight committee lays the groundwork for future hearings or investigation, particularly if control of the chamber changes.

The timing of the CFTC interpretation is legally significant. It came hours after the Ninth Circuit's decision in Blue Lake Rancheria v Kalshi, in which the court unanimously held that Kalshi's sports-event contracts constitute Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act when offered on tribal lands, and found the tribes likely to prove that Kalshi and Polymarket operated without a valid compact. An agency interpretation that would require exchanges to serve those same lands invites a direct clash between the Commodity Exchange Act and IGRA, two federal statutes, rather than the familiar preemption argument between federal and state law.

Chairman Selig has signalled that the CFTC will not retreat. In a televised interview he asserted exclusive federal jurisdiction over DCM-listed event contracts, said the agency would not allow states to sue its exchanges, and indicated a willingness to take the issue to the Supreme Court. He also criticised states pursuing criminal charges against company executives, a reference to Utah Attorney General Derek Brown's filing of 14 criminal counts, 13 of them felonies, against Kalshi's co-founders. Criminal exposure for individuals is a step change in risk that no federal interpretation can fully neutralise.

For operators, the practical dilemma is acute. A DCM that complies with the CFTC interpretation by removing geofences risks contempt of court in states with injunctions, breaches of tribal gaming law and, potentially, criminal liability for executives. A DCM that keeps geofences risks regulatory friction with its federal supervisor. In our view, until a court with jurisdiction rules on the interpretation's validity, the safer course is to continue honouring existing court orders and document the legal basis for doing so. State-licensed sportsbooks and tribal operators should continue to press their positions in pending litigation and in comment opportunities.

The near-term markers to watch are the CFTC's response to the 23 November preservation deadline, any challenge filed against the 5 November interpretation itself, and whether further circuit decisions follow the Ninth Circuit's approach. Legislative action remains unlikely in the short term, but the letter shows that prediction markets are now a cross-party political issue in key gaming states. US gaming and derivatives counsel should be reviewing geofencing and state-access policies now rather than waiting for the Supreme Court.

A.title: Amazon Ads Gambling Policy: Prediction Markets and Licences
A.excerpt: Amazon's revised Gambling and Games policy covers 22 countries and puts prediction markets through the same licence verification as sportsbooks.
body: Amazon Ads published a revised Gambling and Games advertising policy on 12 November 2026, expanding the markets in which gambling advertising is permitted and, notably, bringing prediction markets within the same verification regime as online casinos and sportsbooks. The previous policy allowed gambling advertising in only six countries: Germany, Austria, Spain, France, Italy and the United Kingdom. The new policy contains national sections for 22 countries, including the United States, Canada, Japan, Brazil, Mexico and the UK. Italy is no longer listed, consistent with its broad statutory ban on gambling advertising.

The core of the policy is a licensing gate. Every gambling and games advertiser must be verified by Amazon and must show that its activity is licensed by a regulator or otherwise established as lawful in each country it wishes to target. Advertisers must keep their licences valid throughout a campaign and notify Amazon immediately if a licence is suspended or terminated. Seven categories require verification: online casinos, national or state lotteries, daily fantasy sports, sports betting, online horse racing, offline gambling establishments and prediction markets. Social casino games without real-money wagering or prizes are exempt from verification, though they must still use the Gambling and Sports Betting category.

The treatment of prediction markets is the most consequential element. Amazon has not created a separate policy for event-contract platforms; it classifies them alongside casinos and sportsbooks and applies the same test. In the United States, that raises an immediate question the policy does not answer: does registration as a CFTC designated contract market establish that offering sports event contracts is lawful in a state whose regulator, attorney general or courts say otherwise? With injunctions requiring geofencing in several states and criminal charges filed against executives in Utah, a platform's federal status may not satisfy a test framed around lawfulness in the targeted jurisdiction.

In practice, private platform rules like Amazon's are becoming a parallel layer of licensing enforcement. Google and Meta already require gambling certification in many markets, and regulators increasingly rely on platforms to keep unlicensed operators out of paid media. Amazon's requirement that advertisers report licence suspensions immediately creates a contractual obligation that sits alongside, and may be enforced faster than, any regulatory sanction. A licence suspension in one market could therefore lead to rapid loss of advertising access, and a failure to notify could jeopardise an advertiser's account more broadly.

Content rules also deserve attention. The policy prohibits depicting models or actors who are, or appear to be, under 25, as well as depictions of irresponsible gambling such as chasing losses and deceptive claims. The under-25 threshold mirrors the UK CAP and BCAP codes for people playing a significant role in gambling ads, so UK-compliant creative will largely be suitable. Operators in Brazil, where the SPA's advertising ordinances impose their own restrictions, and in Canadian provinces with their own standards, will need to layer local rules on top of Amazon's baseline. The permitted inventory, which includes Prime Video, Twitch, Live Sports, IMDb and Fire tablets, is subject to restrictions that will matter for live-sport advertising in markets that limit it.

Several gaps remain. The policy page gives no effective date, changelog or transition period, does not say whether existing campaigns must be re-verified, and no longer states the former cap of three gambling impressions per user every 24 hours. The scope and verification lists do not fully align, leaving uncertainty for season-long fantasy contests and private lotteries. Advertisers should seek written confirmation from their Amazon account teams on these points before launching new campaigns rather than relying on silence in the policy text.

For licensed operators, the expansion is a commercial opportunity in markets such as the US, Brazil and Canada, but it comes with a compliance file that must be maintained: current licence evidence for each targeted jurisdiction, internal processes for prompt notification of licence events, and creative review against both Amazon's rules and local codes. Prediction market operators should take advice on how to evidence lawfulness on a state-by-state basis. Gambling advertising and licensing specialists can help build a verification pack that will satisfy both platforms and regulators.
